rationale: Night asks for the songs the mother sang for her child, which supports the reading. The quotation is verbatim but points to Night's view of her tears more than to the bond itself.
The flower brings back the maiden and her words, so the reading is well supported. The quotation is verbatim, but the flower also keeps alive the Danish homeland ('fragrance of the Danish groves').
The trumpeters announce the boy, and the polished balls and rattling armor present the house as alive and welcoming. The quotation is verbatim and directly relevant.

The quotation is verbatim, but the passage widens Cupid's danger to the heartache of love and his cunning disguises, which reach students and maidens who never welcomed him. Betrayed hospitality is only the opening incident.
The reading is supported by 'so uneasy lest he should lose something of his splendor', but the cited wording does not appear in the passage.

The bruises are real, but the passage presents the test as proof of a real princess's sensitivity, not as an exposure of cruelty. The quotation is also not verbatim (the text says 'all over black and blue').
The officer thinks he may be unfit for his office and resolves to hide it, which matches fear of being exposed. The quotation is verbatim and directly relevant.

The ladies object ('we should not like that at all') and the princess invokes her rank, so the reading is supported. The quotation is not verbatim; the text says 'Remember that you owe everything to me.'

Comfort and warmth are explicit ('a world of comfort', 'warmed so delightfully'), and the comfort ends quickly when the flame goes out. The quotation is verbatim but describes the match flame, not the vision.

The quotation is not verbatim (the text says 'How beautiful they were!'). The passage also ties Karen's desire to the princess's shoes and to being looked at, which weakens the claim that visual beauty is the chief driver.
The watchman wants to examine the stars and moon more closely, which supports curiosity. The quotation is verbatim. His musing about souls flying between stars after death adds a second motive.
The passage does ironically warn Denmark not to 'run counter to the moon', but more of the mockery is aimed at the Selenites' self-importance. The quotation is not verbatim.
The Raven calls the tale 'very affecting', but she also asks Gerda to show 'a grateful heart' once she gains honor, which suggests self-interest. The quotation is not verbatim.
The Finland woman says Gerda's power comes from her heart because she is sweet and innocent. The quotation is verbatim and directly relevant.
The shadow tells the princess her overly clear sight has lessened and she is cured, and she happily accepts this, so the reading is supported. The quotation is not verbatim.

The narrator explicitly corrects the collar's boast ('that was not true... but he boasted'), and the quotation is verbatim. The scene also mocks his pushy courtship, so status claims are not the only target.
The procession of crowned kings and queens to the old church supports history and royal continuity, and the quotation is verbatim. The sequence also includes Corsor's civic boasting.

The quotation is verbatim, but the speech promises the young snails they will be 'boiled black, and laid on silver dishes', which reads as ironic vanity rather than plain affection. Father Snail being 'affected' gives only slight support.
'I must and will find the bell' supports personal resolve. The quotation is not verbatim; the text says 'an excellent and resolute youth.'
The Grasshopper's 'ancient Egyptian family', his house of court cards, and the Flea's 'noble blood' all mock absurd claims to rank. The quotation is verbatim and relevant.
